name: Paperforge
tagline: Developer tooling for turning templates plus data into finished documents and PDFs.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Document rendering is one of the most one-shottable categories there is: a headless Chromium, a template engine, and a single POST endpoint covers the happy path in an afternoon. Where DIY builds fall down is everything past the happy path: page breaks that behave, headers and footers with running page numbers, embedded fonts, CJK glyphs, PDF/A output, and a browser process that does not leak memory on document number four thousand. Paid document APIs are mostly selling you a warm rendering farm and a decade of accumulated CSS print hacks, not a clever idea. If you generate invoices for yourself, build it. If you generate other people's legal paperwork, pay someone.
coreLoopDIY: A local HTTP service that takes a template name plus JSON data, renders HTML through headless Chromium, and returns a PDF.
requirements: Node 20+ and roughly 500MB of disk for a Playwright Chromium download
Willingness to debug CSS print rules, which are their own small hell
A machine that stays on if you want the endpoint reachable
whatYouLose: Rendering at scale: one Chromium on your laptop is not a queue with retries and concurrency limits
Battle-tested print CSS edge cases: page breaks inside tables, running footers, widow control
Font and glyph coverage, including non-Latin scripts and licensed typefaces
Compliance-flavored output like PDF/A archival profiles and digital signatures
Hosted template editing and versioning, so non-technical people can tweak a layout without a deploy
moatNotes: The moat is boring and real: someone else keeps the browser farm alive and already knows why your table splits wrong.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because document generation is a chore that looks finished long before it is. The first invoice renders perfectly and the ninetieth one has a stray blank page, a footer that forgot its page number, and a customer name in Thai that comes out as boxes. Paying converts an open-ended maintenance liability into a line item, and it moves the pager for a memory-leaking Chromium process off your desk. For anything customer-facing or billing-related, that trade is usually correct.
notes: Print CSS is the actual product here, and nobody wants to admit it.
prompt:
Build a local document rendering service. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, not negotiable:
- Node 20 with TypeScript
- Fastify for the HTTP layer
- Playwright with bundled Chromium for rendering
- Handlebars for templates
- Local filesystem for templates and output, no database

Behavior:
- Templates live in ./templates/NAME/ with index.hbs and optional style.css and assets/
- POST /render takes JSON: { "template": "invoice", "data": { ... }, "options": { "format": "A4", "margin": "18mm", "landscape": false } }
- Compile the Handlebars template with data, inline style.css, serve local assets over a temporary file URL so images resolve
- Render to PDF with printBackground true, header and footer templates supporting page number and total pages
- Respond with application/pdf and a sane Content-Disposition filename
- POST /render?debug=1 returns the rendered HTML instead of a PDF, for debugging layout
- GET /templates lists available templates
- GET /healthz returns 200 and the Chromium version

Performance and stability:
- Launch one Chromium at boot, reuse it, create a fresh browser context per request
- Cap concurrency at 2 with a simple in-process queue, return 429 when the queue is longer than 20
- Restart the browser automatically after 200 renders or if it crashes
- Hard timeout of 30 seconds per render, always close the context in a finally block

Security and config:
- Require an X-API-Key header matched against API_KEY from .env, loaded with dotenv
- PORT and TEMPLATE_DIR also from .env, ship a .env.example, gitignore .env

Ship with it:
- One working example template: an invoice with a line-item table that repeats table headers across pages
- A test script that renders the example with 200 line items and asserts the PDF has more than one page
- README with curl examples and a short section on print CSS rules that matter: break-inside avoid, thead display table-header-group, @page size

Out of scope, do not build: template web editor, user management, S3 upload, DOCX or XLSX output, PDF/A, digital signatures, webhooks.
